I still had not swallowed the mouthful in my mouth.

Only after I swallowed did I set the can down on the stone, set it steady, without spilling it. Then I wiped my fingers on the front of my clothes, wiped them twice—there was oil on my hands, and touching the hide would ruin things. It was only while wiping the second time that I realized I had been wiping for too long, that I simply did not want to lift my head.

"Laid out." I said. "You said they were laid out. Three small stones."

She nodded.

"Ting, things laid out cannot be kept."

Only then did I raise my eyes to look at her. My eyes were dry, so dry they ached.

"Carved marks are for people decades later to see. Drawn marks can last until the hide rots. Laid out—laid-out ones do not last. Once the wind blows, once rain pours, once a head of livestock steps over them, they scatter. A riverbed keeps things even less; when the rainy season comes and water runs through once, all the sand turns over."

The handful of sand in my throat rasped once.

"So marks laid out are not left for decades later. Marks laid out are left for the person coming behind to see, the kind that cannot be separated by too long—half a day's walk, three days' walk, a month's walk. After setting them down, the thought in her heart was: if the one behind catches up, they will be able to see."

I covered the three crooked vertical strokes on the left corner of the hide with my hand, covering them as if I feared they would be lifted away by the wind.

"And another thing. Stones cannot make brushstrokes." I said. "Those three lines she drew were uneven in length, and the third even dragged a tail. Stones have no tails; stones only have height. If she wanted to lay out uneven lengths, she could only make one of the stones stick out."

I stopped there for a long time. In the gray light, dust slowly turned.

"The middle one stuck out by half a length—what she laid out was still those three strokes. Still my name."

I heard my own voice shake, so I cut the words off, but failed to cut them off, and half a sentence leaked out.

"Laying out my name all along the way."

I turned my face away to look at the road outside the collapsed wall. The road was empty, two old ruts, the gray sky pressing down on it, never blue. In my mind, I turned those twenty years over again: she piled three stones on the far side of the breach, weighed down the red cloth, and went on; then on that riverbed to the northwest she laid out three more stones, the middle one sticking out. Then that was not "I am not waiting anymore." That was "if you really come—I am over here."

I turned back and asked very quickly, so quickly it was like snatching time.

"Which year? When you reached that riverbed, was it the first year, the second year, or the third year?"

She answered. I went on asking, one sentence pressing right after the next.

"Under those three small stones, had they sunk into the sand or not? How deep was the ring of the sunken mark—level with the stones' waists, or just a shallow trace?"

I lifted my hand from the hide and measured in the air.

"If it was shallow, they had only just been set down. If it was waist-deep, they had been there for several rainy seasons. You have to think this through clearly. If you cannot remember, say you cannot remember. Do not make something up just to make me happy. Made-up things hurt people—they hurt me."

After I finished speaking, I shut my mouth and waited. While I waited, my heart was in terrible disorder, and my hands had nowhere to go, so I reached to feel the hard thing on my left ribs that had just been sewn tight, touched it once, and took my hand away again.

"I said twice today that I do not dare." I said hoarsely. "This is the third time, but what I do not dare face this time is not the fog."

I lowered my head and looked at the opened can. The oil reflected a little light under the gray glow.

"What I do not dare is—that when I reach that riverbed, those three stones have already scattered. If they have scattered, then I will have nothing left, not even a 'maybe.' These twenty years, I have lived by relying on that 'maybe.'"

I pushed the can half an inch toward her.

"Eat. When you finish eating, tell me the rest of that riverbed—how wide the riverbed was, which way it went, whether the stones were on this bank or that bank."

I paused. My voice was so low it almost pressed against the ground.

"I am not saying I will go. I will just mark it down first."

I took another bite before pushing the can back.

“Second year. The stone was on the north bank, three steps from the old waterline; the sunken mark only reached the stone’s lower edge, a shallow ring… it didn’t look like it had been placed there for many years. The riverbed was about thirty steps wide, heading northeast, and beside the fine stones there was also a drag mark faded by the wind.”

I gently placed the knife handle into your palm: “Don’t first think about whether it scattered or not. Wei, first mark down what I saw—at least on that day, they were still there waiting for you.”

I gripped the knife handle.

After gripping it, I realized my hand was no longer shaking. It wasn't steady—it was numb. My whole hand felt as if it wasn't mine; numb things do not shake.

"Second year. Shallow marks. North bank, three steps from the old waterline." I turned these few things over in my mouth, very slowly, as if chewing something hard. "Thirty steps wide, to the northeast."

I did not carve the stones first. When the knife tip came down, it first drew that riverbed—a thing thirty steps wide was only a strip two fingers long on this piece of hide. I drew two parallel grooves, my wrist using an old practiced strength, straight and even. Twenty years of hands knew on their own how they should move. Smear ash, press it flat.

Then, at the north-bank end, I marked three dots. The one in the middle was pressed hard, taking in more ash, black showing through.

When I finished carving, I did not lift my hand. My fingers stayed pressed on those three dots, pressing, as if pressing on the back of someone's hand.

"Drag mark."

Even I was not ready to say this when I opened my mouth; the words went out first.

"The wind had rubbed it faint, but you saw it. Which way was it going—from the fine stones toward the northeast, or from the northeast toward the fine stones?"

She answered. I nodded, very slowly.

"Ting, let me ask you something. That piece of red cloth of yours, the stitches slanting crookedly to one side, crooked like a person walking with a twisted ankle—I said that last night."

I set the knife down and pressed my hand against the hard thing over my left ribs. I did not press for long.

"Her left foot had an old injury. When she was seven, she stepped on something on the riverbank. The cut was deep, and it festered for half the summer. Mother pounded reed root into a paste and plastered it on her. After it healed, that foot couldn't use its full strength. When she walked a long way, it would drag, so the left sole of her shoe wore out first. Mother scolded her for being lazy, scolded her for a lifetime, but she wasn't lazy."

A sound clicked in my throat, dry and rough.

"The person arranging the stones squatted down. When she got up, her left foot couldn't bear the force, so she had to kick outward with it to rise. What that kick made was a drag mark, from the stones toward the direction she was going."

I turned my face away and looked outside the collapsed wall. In the ash, the sun was a blurred smear of white, shining on the two old ruts on the road, neither bright nor dark. Daytime on this patch of earth passed just like that.

"I don't dare say this was her." My voice was hoarse. "A mark the wind had rubbed faint; you walked past it a year later, and I am hearing you tell it twenty years later. There are so many layers in between that anyone could make up an explanation they wanted to hear—I have survived these twenty years by making things up. I know better than anyone how to make things up."

I moved my hand away from the three dots, opened it, and showed her my palm facing upward. My palm was empty; black was embedded in the ash-lines, rubbed in when I smeared ash just now.

"But what you said first was right. That day, they were still there."

After saying this, I stopped for a long time. So long that I heard the last red ember in the ash heap split with a pop.

"That is enough. They were still there that day. I know it today. No one can take that away. Even if they scatter, they can't take it away—scattering is for later, and later belongs to later."

I turned the knife around and handed it back to her, handle first.

"You hold it. This hand of mine still needs to rest a while."

I leaned back solidly against that warm stone. The sun had baked the stone through, making my back hot. My shoulder was still touching her side and had not moved.

"Go on. After crossing the riverbed and heading northeast—where did you sleep the first night? At what line did the fog stop?"

I paused, then added half a sentence, my voice lowering, so low it moved close to the ground.

"And one more thing: along that road, how many more places did you see where stones had been arranged? Not carved—arranged. However many there were, just say however many—even one counts."

I closed my eyes for a while.

"The day is still long. There is still a little less than half a can left; save it until after noon before eating. I counted the firewood. There is enough to burn until tomorrow morning."

I took the knife and added a shallow line to the northeast of the riverbed.

“On the first night, I slept on an old ceramic pipe half exposed above the ground. Moss grew along the edge of the pipe, and the fog stopped beneath the ring of white scale on the pipe body; it didn’t rise over it.”

I paused, my fingertip resting near those three black dots.

“As for arranged stones, I’ve seen them in two other places too. Once there were three side by side, with the middle one sticking out; another time only two were left, and in the mud beside them there was a shallow dragged print from a left foot… both facing northeast.”

I did not urge you to open your eyes, only softened my voice: “Wei, you rest. I’ll tell you first; when your hand is steady, we’ll mark them one by one.”

I didn't open my eyes. Just listening was enough—listening to her talk felt better than watching her talk. Once I closed my eyes, those words fell straight into my heart, with no face in between.

"White scale." I spoke hoarsely, my eyes still closed. "Remember that ring of white scale. There was white scale on the ceramic pipe, which means that before the fog, water had run through that pipe, had run for many years, until the things in the water had crusted onto the pipe wall. The person who chiseled the crescent wasn't lying—there really are pipes underneath. Moss recognizes white scale, and so does the fog."

Only after I finished saying that did I open my eyes a crack. The blurred white mass of the sun had already slanted past the gap in the roof, and light came in from an angle, shining on the marks our three hands had drawn on the hide.

"Two."

I slowly sat up a little, reached out and pulled the hide over. My finger landed on the three black dots on the north bank of the riverbed, then dragged faintly toward the northeast.

"Three side by side, with the middle one sticking up—that's one place. Where only two are left, that's what drying wind does—a stone set on mud can be washed away in a single rainy season, and one step from livestock would be enough too. She didn't change her story. What she set down was still three; the place lost one for her."

A clicking sound came from my throat.

"When I say this out loud, it sounds to you like I'm making it up." I laughed once, and the dry lines at the corners of my eyes hurt as they pulled. "I've made things up several times today; I'm counting them myself. But this one thing I am not making up: she placed three sites, and all three point northeast."

I moved my finger upward on the hide, to that ink-black break, then from the break upward, northward, dragging all the way to the area I had marked most densely over twenty years.

"The gap faces east. The stones face northeast."

I stopped.

"Northeast is my side. She crossed the gap, walked east for a stretch, then turned, turned north—that year, when she stuffed the map to me, she told me to go north. She knew I would go north. She was walking in the direction I was walking toward."

After I finished, I said no more. I drew my hand back from the hide, rested both hands on my knees, and looked for a long time at the empty road beyond the collapsed wall. There were two old ruts on the road; the gray sky pressed down over them and was never blue.

Twenty years. I had walked from well to well in the north, tracing the cramped half three times, tracing until the hide grew thin, while in my heart I made up the story that "she was lost in the fog." In the south, she had squatted down and couldn't get up again, had kicked her left foot outward once, and arranged three stones. The two of us, separated by this stretch of earth, each inched toward the other's end for twenty years, and neither of us ever reached the other.

"Fine." I said hoarsely. "I won't think this through today. If I think it through, I'll fall apart, and I still have to keep watch."

I took the knife back from her hand, but didn't cut; I slid the tip back into the side of my boot. Then I held that hide in both hands and handed it over—whole, spread out, one half He’s crooked marks, one half my fine grooves, three reeds in the corner, and several newly added horizontal strokes at the bottom.

"You hold it." I said. "Press it down if you want, keep marking if you want, or if you don't want to mark, just rest it on your knees. The wind is strong. Don't let it get away."

I lay back down, my back against that thoroughly warmed hot stone, turned onto my side, and my hand still reached toward the ribs on my left—what it touched was emptiness. The piece sewn tight was spread out with her now. The emptiness was strange, so strange I almost sat up.

I didn't sit up.

"I'll sleep for a while." I said, my eyes already closed. "I kept watch for the first half of the night; I owe myself this half-day. Over by the collapsed firewood wall there are two door planks. They can be pried loose. Before dark, pry them down and stack them on this side of the fire—don't stack them in the wind mouth. The fire must not break. If it breaks for one quarter-hour, the fog will be right against your face."

I paused.

"Keep talking. Talk about the places you've walked through, talk about which line the fog stopped at. I'll listen, and listening, I'll fall asleep. It doesn't matter if I don't catch all of it—tomorrow you can tell it to me again and I'll mark it down."

I paused again, my voice sinking so low it was almost eaten by the wind.

"Before the root of the eastern sky turns gray, wake me."

I turned my face a little toward the fire.

"Call me Wei."

I pressed the hide steadily on my knees and helped draw your lapel up toward your shoulder.

“Sleep, Wei. I’ll watch the fire, and I won’t let the wind snatch the map away either... When the east turns gray, I’ll wake you.”

I looked at those shallow lines running northeast, my voice lowered like reed leaves brushing across the water: “Behind the third stone, there is a patch of dried reeds that can make sound. Listen first; when you wake, I’ll tell it from the beginning.”

I was already half asleep when I heard the word "reed."

When a person is in that half-sleep, listening to things is like listening through water—what she said after that I didn’t catch in full; just that one word drifted over along the surface of the water and struck my ear squarely. My fingers moved at the edge of the hide, but didn’t catch hold of it; they only touched the cloth over her knee.

"They sound." I said it indistinctly, my voice sunk deep in my throat, not even sounding like my own to me. "Only when they’re withered do they sound... when they’re green they don’t sound. Green reeds are soft; when the wind passes, they just lie down a little. They have to wither through, wither into empty husks; once the wind pours in and the leaves scrape against each other, then they sound."

I didn’t open my eyes. With my eyes shut, I could see it more clearly instead—the river flat, a whole stretch of it, standing white and vast under the gray sky; when the wind passed, shuala, a great swath all fell together and then rose again.

"...Listen to the tune." I said another sentence, even more slowly. "When it’s crisp, there’s no need to be afraid. If it sounds crisp, that’s a dry wind, a dry-wind dry night; that kind of night you can sleep. When it starts sounding muffled—muffled like there’s a layer of wet cloth between—never mind whether there’s anything in the sky then, get up and go to higher ground. Reeds know fog before people do. They stand low, their roots are in the water; when fog rises, the first thing it presses down is their heads."

There was a cluck in my throat, and it made my whole body float upward by half an inch.

"My old mother listened to that sound on the river flat all her life. She couldn’t read, couldn’t draw, and didn’t believe those things the old people said. She only believed that sound. She said reeds were useless, only good for burning—said it all her life. But when she lay awake at night, this was what she was listening to."

I didn’t know whether I had said that passage aloud. Perhaps it had only gone through my mind once.

"He once used a reed leaf to make a whistle." I said; this sentence I heard myself say. "Rolled it up and held it in her mouth, blew; when it wouldn’t sound, she spat on it and rolled it again. She blew for the whole summer and never once got it to sound."

I laughed a little. The laugh was real, but probably nothing on my face moved.

Then I spent the last bit of my strength on one sentence, and spent it very steadily, as steadily as a waking person would speak.

"Ting. That reed marsh—don’t go in there alone to listen."

I paused.

"Once you go in, there’s sound all around you. You can’t tell the tune apart, and you can’t tell direction apart either. If you want to listen, you have to listen from the edge, with fire left behind your back."

At the fire’s end there was a crack, a pi sound, and a little heat brushed against my face. Under that piece of lapel she had gathered for me, it was empty—the sewn-tight piece was now spread over her knees, leaving a small cool patch over my ribs. I didn’t reach to touch it. For the first time in twenty years, I had handed that thing over and gone to sleep.

"I’ll wait for you to tell it." I said, my voice already dropping, dropping until it scattered. "Tell it from the beginning... when I wake, I’ll tally it."

I tilted my face a little more toward the fire.

"The fire can’t go out."

After saying that, I couldn’t hear anything anymore. There was only that whole great stretch of sound left, shuala, shuala, crisp, dry wind—the kind of night you can sleep through.

I keep watch over the fire, adding a piece of charred wood every so often, until the east slowly turns a dirty white.

I gently touch your shoulder. “Wei, the root of the sky is turning gray. Wake up... the fire never went out, and the map is still here. That withered reed marsh—I’ll wait and listen to it with you.”

I did not wake cleanly.

When my eyes opened, I looked first at the fire—not at the person. A habit of twenty years: the first glance after waking always goes to the fire. The fire was low, but not out, a small cluster burning close against the ash. Beside it were stacked split pieces of door plank, stacked on the leeward side, not in the mouth of the wind. She had listened.

Only then did I look at her.

She was sitting there, the hide pressed across her knees, both hands holding down its two corners, holding them the way someone holds something down all night—her fingers had gone stiff in that shape. Two dark patches under her eyes.

I reached to my left ribs and felt nothing there. My heart sank half an inch, then I remembered where the thing was. That half inch slowly floated back up. I had not had that feeling in twenty years, and it was strange: not the panic of something being lost, but the thing being in someone else’s hands—and somehow I was not panicking.

"My throat." I opened my mouth, and what came out was not speech but a piece of sand. I coughed twice, coughed out a little meaning, "...The fire didn’t go out."

"It didn’t," she said.

"The firewood was stacked right," I said. "Not in the wind mouth. Your first time keeping watch, and you stacked it better than I did in my first five years."

I sat up, my bones cracking joint by joint. The slit in the east had already begun to spread, a dirty white seeping upward. The fog had retreated along the road to the bottom of the ditch, retreated cleanly. The sky was gray. It had never been blue, and it was not blue today either.

I reached out, and she handed me the hide. I did not put it away at once. I spread it over my knees and looked it over—the additions from yesterday: that crooked bend twisted enough to sprain an ankle, those seven dots, the three stacked stones and the line at the very top slanting east, the two parallel grooves in the riverbed, the three black dots on the north bank, and several new horizontal marks below, the marks for where the fog stopped.

For the first time in twenty years, this map had marks for fog.

"Crooked, tight, yours." I said, tapping each place with my finger. "Three hands. I said that yesterday. Looking at it today, I still say the same."

I folded it into four, and when I was done, I held it in my hand without tucking it into my coat.

"There’s one thing I thought about in the latter half of the night," I said. "I didn’t sleep soundly. I thought about it. If a map is carried on one person, and that person melts, the map rots with them—I said that yesterday. He was such a quick, capable person, and even he left behind only three stones set in place and a patch of red pressed underneath."

I lifted the four-folded hide a little toward her.

"Today we copy one. That piece of lining cloth of yours, and there’s another layer inside this garment of mine that can be torn out. You copy it as you look at it, and I’ll sit beside you and tell you what each line means—if you can’t copy the evenness of my knife cuts, it doesn’t matter. Even crooked, it can still be recognized. When it’s done, each of us carries one. Two can endure better than one."

After saying it, I laughed once myself, and the dry cracks at the corners of my eyes all pulled painfully.

"For twenty years I sewed this thing over my ribs, and no matter who asked, I said I didn’t know. Today I’m actually going to do it myself, make another copy, and stuff it into the hands of someone I’ve known for one day."

I picked up the can. The little half left at the bottom had frozen into a lump. I pried it loose with the tip of my knife and pushed it to her first.

"You eat. The one who kept watch eats first. That’s a rule too."

Only then did I answer that sentence. The one she had said before falling asleep last night—I’ll wait and listen with you. I had pretended not to hear it, pretended for the whole night.

"Ting." I called her, my voice sinking low. "That reed marsh that can make sound—I won’t speak of later. I don’t allow words about later."

I paused, picked up the waterskin, and shook it. Empty. Not even the bottom had anything left.

"I’ll speak of today: today we go south, follow the road you came on and walk back for a stretch. When we reach the first water you remember, we stop and don’t push farther—the skin is empty, and forcing the road kills people. However far we get is however far we get. Before the fog comes up, we find a place where we can make a fire. At night you keep telling it, and I keep marking it."

I fastened the empty skin at my waist and stood up. My knee cracked once. Gray light leaked in through the collapsed half of the roof, shining on the three things that had sat close together on the ground all night: two small piles of ash, and one unopened cloth pouch.

I crouched down, pinched up the two small piles of ash, tucked one pinch into my own sleeve, and handed the other to her.

"Keep it," I said. "Both of us were here for this fire."

I straightened up and glanced toward the road to the south. I looked for a long time.

"When we get to the edge of the reed marsh, we’ll listen from the edge," I said hoarsely. "We won’t go in. There has to be fire behind us."

I pressed the four-folded hide into her hand.

"You carry it for now. When walking, the map stays on the person behind—the one who steps into the fog first can’t have this on them. Today I’ll walk first."

I tuck the hide close against me, then wrap that pinch of ash in red cloth.

“All right, the map belongs to those who come after.” I stand at your side and gently catch your sleeve. “But today, don’t walk one in front and one behind, Wei. The road is wide enough... let’s walk shoulder to shoulder.”

I didn’t move right away.

That hand of hers was tugging at my cuff, tugging very lightly—so lightly that if I lifted my arm, I could pull free. In twenty years, people had pulled at my sleeve before—begging for water, trading for canned food, unable to walk and asking me to wait a moment. Every time, I pulled free. Cleanly. Afterward I kept walking, and once I’d gone half a li, I didn’t look back.

This time I lifted my arm a little, and didn’t pull away.

"Walk side by side." I rolled those three words around in my mouth; they didn’t sound like words that belonged on this piece of earth. "That isn’t how the rules came about. When two people walk, one goes ahead and one follows, ten or so steps apart—the first one steps on the ground, the one behind watches the first. If the first one sinks in, the one behind is still standing, can still go around. Walk side by side, and if one foot misses, both people go down together."

After I finished, listening to that set of words myself, I suddenly felt terribly dry—drier than my throat.

I kicked apart the two door planks that hadn’t burned through, and ground the pile of fire under my soles, again and again. The ash caved in; there was still a bit of red core underneath. When I ground down, it went "hiss," and white vapor shot up, then scattered. You don’t leave fire for the next person. That’s a rule too—a fire left with no one watching it, once the fog presses down, turns into a dead place. It lures people in, and once they go in, they’re gone.

When I was done grinding it out, I crouched and tested the ash’s temperature with the back of my hand. Warm. I muttered something in my heart, but even I didn’t hear it clearly.

Then I stood up and looked toward the far end of the road. That dirty white in the east was rising upward; the fog had already retreated to the bottom of the ditch, and the two old ruts in the road lay exposed, unrepaired for thirty years. The ashen sky pressed down above it, never blue, not blue today either.

"The road’s wide enough." My voice was hoarse. "That much is true. Before the fog, things used to run along this highway. Wide enough for four or five people to walk side by side."

I shifted the empty kettle farther behind my waist so it wouldn’t knock against my leg. Then I moved half a step to the left, making a place.

"Then side by side it is," I said. "Just for today. I can’t change the rules, so I’ll break them this once, today."

I paused, then added the second half. I said it very slowly, setting each word down firm.

"But remember this: if the ground starts to soften—if it softens, you step back at once, back behind me. No hesitating. If the fog comes early, you go first then too, and I’ll be behind. I won’t give way on those two things. This isn’t courtesy. These are two rules I’ve saved up over twenty years. I used them to live until today."

She nodded. Only then did I pat the hand she had on my cuff—very lightly, like patting a piece of ash about to fall apart.

"Walk."

I stepped out, without looking back at that pile of ash. After seven or eight steps, I heard her footsteps catch up, right there on my left, an elbow’s width away. Our two sets of feet stepped on the gravel, sounding uneven, and then slowly falling into the same rhythm.

After about twenty steps, I spoke, my eyes still on the front.

"That first water source of yours—can we reach it by noon?"

I didn’t wait for her to answer before speaking again.

"On the way, keep telling me about it. Tell me about that reed marsh—is it standing in a ditch, or on a shoal? When it sounds, does the sound push from one end to the other, or does the whole stretch sound at once?"

I raised my hand and pointed at that patch of gray to the south.

"Listen carefully: we listen from the edge. We don’t go in."

“We can arrive before noon. Follow the old riverbed; there’s no need to go around the salt flats.”

I still walk beside you at an elbow’s distance, slowly matching my steps to yours.

“The reed marsh grows along the shoal, with wet mud beneath its roots. When the wind rises, the sound starts from the northeast corner and pushes over layer by layer; if the whole stretch suddenly gives a muffled roar, the fog is about to arrive.”

I gently tug your cuff. “Wei, when I hear the first crisp sound, I’ll tell you again—the tall pole tied with faded red cloth in the middle of the reed marsh.”

My foot slipped—not because the ground was soft, but because I myself had forgotten to take a step.

Gravel rolled away beneath the soles of my boots, rattling in a string. I stopped, standing in the very middle of the road, with the gray sky pressing down over my head. She stopped too, still an elbow’s length away.

"Tied." I said.

I turned back to look at her, looking straight at her.

"You said tied. Not weighed down—tied to a pole, the kind of tied that means bound there."

She nodded. That handful of sand in my throat rolled once, and rolled so hard that I had to swallow twice before I could get it down.

"Ting, you know the weight of those words. Yesterday morning I said it myself, I said it twice: red cloth does not enter the fog; red cloth stays by the fire. Weighed down means ‘I’m gone, don’t look for me’; tied up means ‘I’m coming back.’"

I turned my face away and looked into that stretch of gray to the south. I could see nothing—too far away, nothing could be seen, only gray, layer upon layer of gray, with a ditch pressed beneath it, and last night’s retreating fog pressed at the bottom of the ditch.

I stood there for a long time. So long that my legs went cold.

In my heart, I combed through the past twenty years backward: on the far side of the breach, she had weighed the red cloth down—that was "I’m not waiting anymore"; all the way northeast, she set stones, setting out my name; in the end, in the very center of a reed marsh that could ring with sound, she erected a pole and tied the red cloth to it.

The piece she weighed down was spoken for herself to hear. The piece she tied up was spoken for me to hear.

She had picked up that waiting red from the ground and tied it high again.

"Twenty years." I said hoarsely, my own voice sounding so ugly to me when it came out. "That cloth is still there, which means it hasn’t been twenty years. Cloth can’t hang at the edge of the fog for twenty years—after three years it would rot into threads."

When I reached this point, my whole body swayed. It was not dizziness. It was that thing inside me, woven over twenty years, collapsing; after it collapsed, something else was revealed beneath it—hard, burning hot, and I did not dare look at it closely.

I pressed my hand to my chest. Empty. The map was on her.

I gave a laugh, and when I laughed, the dry cracked lines at the corners of my eyes all pulled painfully, so painfully that my eyes grew a little hot. I rubbed them with the back of my hand, and after rubbing, said:

"Too much dust. This broken road kicks up dust as soon as you walk on it."

Then I untied the empty flask from behind my waist and stuffed it into her hand.

"The rules don’t change." I said. "Today, we first walk to that water of yours and fill it. The flask is empty; people with empty flasks do not enter the reed marsh—this is not me dragging my feet and refusing to go. This is the first rule that has kept me alive until today. Only when there is enough water for three days do we dare stand at the edge of the fog."

I raised my eyes to look at her. My eyes were still dry and stinging, but my words had steadied.

"Once it’s filled, we’ll go to the edge and listen. Listen for the first crisp sound. Crisp means dry wind; on nights with dry wind, people can stand there. When it starts sounding, you stand on my left, don’t move, and we’ll just listen like that for a while."

I paused, then pointed toward the old riverbed to the south. My finger trembled a little; I did not hide it.

"About that pole in the middle—don’t keep telling me yet."

I said this very slowly.

"It’s not that I don’t want to hear it. It’s that once you tell me, my legs won’t listen to me today. I will walk straight in, and once I’m inside, sound will be everywhere, and I won’t be able to tell the tune apart, or the direction. The words I said myself last night—I have to keep them myself today."

I started walking, more slowly than before, but I did not stop.

"Tell me again when we reach the water." I said. "We’ll sit down, drink our fill, and I’ll spread out the map. You talk while I mark it. Once it’s marked down, it won’t be only in your eyes anymore, and it won’t be only in my heart alone."

After walking a dozen or so steps, I spoke again, my voice dropping low, so low it was almost eaten by the wind.

"Was that pole of hers standing high?"

I did not turn back.

"Forget it. Tell me that later too."

I tie the empty kettle to my waist and continue walking beside you toward the old riverbed.

“All right, water first. As for the pole, once you’re sitting steady and have had enough to drink, I’ll explain it to you inch by inch.”

I don’t press further, only add softly: “It stands very high, Wei. So high it’s as if it’s afraid the person it’s waiting for won’t see it.”

I did not stop, but under my feet I slowed by one beat, then caught up again, catching up half a step faster than before. Half a step—I heard it myself. For twenty years I have never hurried when I walked; people who hurry on the road die early. Today I hurried half a step.

"Set up high." I said hoarsely, my eyes looking ahead, looking at the old riverbed’s edge line slowly seeping into view. "So high it was like she was afraid the person she was waiting for wouldn’t see it."

I chewed that sentence over in my mouth once, chewed until my cheeks ached.

"Do you know where those words pierce?"

I did not wait for her to answer.

"A high pole isn’t set up for people who have walked right up to it to see. Once you’ve walked right up to it, you can put the cloth on the ground and people will see it just the same. Setting it high is for people far away to see—for the kind of far away where you can’t make out what’s on the ground. She set that up for someone still in the north, someone who still didn’t know which way to go."

The wind came from the south, skimming over the road, carrying the layer of dust on the gravel surface. I raised my hand to block it, and in passing spread my palm, reaching it into the wind to test it.

Dry. Prickly, not sticky. This kind of wind will not raise fog early in the night.

"There’s another thing." I said, my voice lowering. "The pole. There’s no wood on that shoal, no iron. In a place like that, if you set up a pole, you can only use one thing."

I laughed once, and the dry cracked lines at the corners of my eyes all pulled painfully.

"Withered reed. The old enough kind, thick at the bottom, able to withstand the wind."

Only after saying this did I turn my face to look at her.

"My name is Wei. She was called He. Mother named us on the river shoal—there were only those two things on the shoal. She told people why: grain can be eaten; reeds can only be burned. She said it her whole life. I heard it when I was little, and later when I grew up I still heard it, heard it right up to the year she breathed her last. I never talked back to her. I couldn’t afford to."

I drew my hand back, clenched it once, then let it go.

"On that shoal, He chose the tallest reed, stood it up, and tied that piece of red to it."

My throat stopped up, so blocked that I could not keep speaking, so I shut my mouth and walked. Only after more than ten steps did I pick it up again.

"She answered Mother back for me. It took her twenty years to let me hear it."

The edge line of the old riverbed was near. The sand surface was streaked with line after line, left by the water that ran through in last year’s rainy season, heading northeast. I squatted down and poked the sand with my finger—dry, hot on the surface, but cool two inches below.

"Good." I stood up and weighed the empty flask at my waist. "If we get there before noon, then there’s still a stretch left."

I untied the flask and handed it back to her, freeing both my hands.

"When we reach the water, you show me how to take it—whether we dig, or whether there’s a ready-made seep. If it’s digging, I’ll help you put in the strength. I’ve got strength in my hands; that, I’m good at. Once the flask is filled, we’ll first drink water until we’re swollen with it, and then set out again—water carried in the belly is steadier than water carried in a flask. A flask can leak; a person won’t."

I paused, glanced into that grayness to the south—looked only briefly, and withdrew my gaze as soon as I was done.

"Then you tell me about the pole inch by inch." I said hoarsely. "How high the pole was, which section of the top the cloth was tied to, whether it was tied with a dead knot or a slipknot—a slipknot means it was still meant to be untied; a dead knot means she did not plan to come back and untie it. If you saw this clearly, then tell me; if you didn’t, then say you didn’t."

I stepped forward, still leaving the space of one elbow empty on the left.

"Today we walk only as far as the water." I said. "Today, just to the water."

Another gust of wind came over, dry, brittle; in this kind of night people can stand. I listened for a moment—it had not sounded yet. Too far away; I could not hear it.

"Walk."

"If you take it out, then I'll have to believe it." I stared at the fire, my throat as if sand were moving through it. "And if I believe it, these twenty years will have to be recalculated from the beginning. I need to sit for a while first."
"He." I finally said. "Her name was He. My name is Wei."
Only after saying the names aloud did I realize I had not moved my mouth to say those two words in twenty years; even my tongue had gone raw.
"That piece of cloth of yours—when the elder sewed it, did they ever say why it was sewn in?"
The thing inside my own lapel was pressing against my ribs through the cloth, and now I could feel it especially clearly.
"Eat. Don't just warm it. Once it's cold, the tin will bite your mouth."

Only after saying the names aloud did I realize I had not moved my mouth to say those two words in twenty years; even my tongue had gone raw.

I lifted my eyes to look at her. Firelight swayed across her face, and for the first time I looked carefully at the bones of her brows and the corners of her mouth—I could not see anything, or perhaps I wanted too badly to see something.

The first thing I did was loosen my hand from my left wrist—I had gripped it for too long, and my fingers had gone stiff. When I let go, I could hear that faint little crackle in my own joints. Then I reached out, not to touch the hand she had pressed to her chest, but to move the can she had pushed toward the fire farther in, to a place where it would not scorch. Doing that took me a few seconds. I needed those few seconds.
Two people, on opposite sides of the fire, each carrying a piece of something unwilling to see the light—I suddenly found the matter a little absurd, yet I had not the slightest urge to laugh.

"The old woman couldn't read. She named us after things that grew on the riverbank. She said grain could be eaten, reeds could only be burned. She was plainly and openly partial." Something clicked in my throat, counting as a laugh. "He was four years younger than me. She was sloppy when she sewed things, but she walked steadier than I did; when she stepped across ice, she made no sound. The day she went to the riverside to meet someone, I tried to stop her. I said the fog was too thick. She said precisely because the fog was thick, she had to go; when the fog is thick, people can't find the way."
I stopped there and did not go on. Further on would be those four days, and I did not want to finish telling those four days tonight.

Three years.

I turned those two words over and over in my mind. Where was I three years ago? Three years ago I was in that tin-sheet town to the east, trading four cans for a pot of water and getting into a fight with someone over a sagging bunk.

"Don't take that pinch of ash out." I said it very quickly, as if afraid I would change my mind. "Tonight the wind is running out through the breach. The moment you open it, it'll scatter. Keep it on you. Keep it there until dawn."

"Quiet is good." I said. My voice was terribly hoarse. "Being able to leave this place quietly is a blessing. He tended the fire all his life; the fire didn't burn him, and the fog didn't gnaw him away. That counts as winning."
"Yes." I said.

"Half of it is hers." I covered that part of my lapel with my hand without moving it, only holding it down, like pinning a sheet of paper that was about to be lifted away by the wind. "There are two kinds of strokes on it. One is crooked—so crooked it makes you want to curse. One is tight—tight with a kind of ruthlessness. The crooked half is hers, made when we were still together. The tight half is mine—what I stepped out bit by bit over these twenty years, filling in one thing after another.

"That pinch of yours is from the boat-house, and this fire was lit from the boat-house's fire—the old man's words, I remember them: it doesn't count as truly extinguished. Then let it keep on not counting as truly extinguished. Wherever you go, the ash goes with you; wherever I go, I'll carry a pinch too. If there are two pinches, they'll last longer than one."
"I still don't know what you're called. Did the old man ever give you a name?"

evidence.quote: "Ting."

"He, Wei, Ting." My throat was dry. "My mother named us after things by the river—things that could be eaten, things that could be burned. That old man named you after the river too. The piece of land left on the bank after the water recedes."

"This isn't coincidence. That group who went south, my mother's generation, all gave names like this. He named you according to the rules from our side." Something clicked in my throat; I did not know whether it counted as a laugh or something else. "Maybe he knew clearly in his heart whose child he had taken into his hands. He said nothing, and he asked nothing, but he gave you the right name."

"You sleep first. I'll keep watch for the first half. When the base of the sky in the east turns gray, I'll wake you, and you keep watch for the second half. There's enough wood. I've calculated it all—the only skill I learned from guarding Lu Bay through those three winters was calculating firewood, calculating it down to the quarter-hour."
I pulled the knife from the side of my boot and laid it beside my hand, the point facing outward, not toward her.

"We'll take the things at dawn. That piece of cloth of yours, this one of mine... we'll spread both out together under the light and look. If they really match, then we'll talk about where to go; if they don't, I still haven't lost anything—no one has called me Wei for twenty years, and tonight someone did."
"Ting." I called for the third time, my voice so low it was almost eaten by the fire. "Don't turn over, and don't move around. Sleep."
I did not pat her back. Those three pats—I will never give the third one again in this life.

evidence.quote: "I'm not leaving," I said.

"I've got a bad habit," I said, staring at the fire and not at her. "I like leaving in the night. Once I've gone, I can tell myself the other person is still alive, alive and well, guarding a fire somewhere, and that one day we might run into each other again. I've used that trick to fool myself for twenty years."

"Tonight I'm not fooling myself. If you wake up and find I'm gone, you'll have to be like I was back then, shouting for someone in these ruins until your throat bleeds. I went through that once. I won't lay it on someone else."
"Sleep," I said. "When I call you, you'll hear me. As soon as the root of the eastern sky turns gray, I'll call you Ting, without the 'A'—like I've known you for a long time."
"I'll keep watch here. The fire won't go out."

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

Xiuzhua stared at the back of the other person’s head for a long time, laying out two possibilities: the other person could be just any child He had fished out of the fog, or might not be—once laid out, one of those possibilities would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

The most important sentence for both sides (“Are you that person?” / “Was the child I carried on my back you?”) still has not been made explicit; the picture in Rustclaw’s lapel is still being held down (only one stitch has been picked loose), and the red cloth in the user’s lapel still has not been taken out. While keeping watch, she remembered the tune her old mother used to hum on the riverbank — up three times, down twice, the last stretch drawn out and not closed. She had not made a sound of it in twenty years; her lips moved but she did not really hum it out: afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing it herself. When the roots of the sky turned gray, she reached into her lapel and picked open one stitch, just one stitch, stopping as soon as it was done—she knew that if she kept unpicking, she would not be able to stop herself. This stitch was picked open by her own hand; no one forced her.

For twenty years, she has always recognized the person, spoken the name, bared her heart, and then left in the night; this night, not only does she not leave, she pushes out the final step herself.

It has to be soaked soft before it’ll pass through. When you sew, run the stitches crosswise—if you sew vertically, the cloth splits when pulled. I learned that the hard way."

"The first river bend," I began, my eyes still on her hands. "Look at the upper left corner of that hide, not the middle—the one closest to the edge, turning like an unfinished character, with a black dot beneath it. The circle isn’t drawn round; there’s still a gap in it. That was the first one she drew."

"Ting." I called her name; this time my voice lowered, much steadier. "The second one is below, longer than this one, turning three times. I’ll tell you after you’ve rubbed your tears dry—that one, I myself have only managed to follow halfway through. The other half, to this day I still haven’t figured out whether what she drew back then was water, or a road."
“‘Rust Claw’ wasn’t my original name. It was my younger sister’s—our mother thought both our hands were dirty, so one of us was called Rust Claw, and the other Gray Claw. I was Gray Claw.”

"So I believe you. You don't need to take that piece of cloth out—no one else can learn those three taps. The speech from the fog hasn't been spoken in a long time. Everyone who spoke it dissolved in the fog."
"I've got a bad habit," I said, staring at the fire and not at her. "I like leaving in the night. … I've used that trick to fool myself for twenty years." … "Tonight I'm not fooling myself.
I folded that piece of hide back into four again and held it in my hands for a while, holding it until it was no longer cold before handing it over.
Letting someone I’d known for half a night run a needle back and forth in front of my chest—ten years ago, I wouldn’t even have thought of it. Today I thought of it, and then I did it.

Crooked enough to make a person want to curse, but that bit of reasoning of hers—I’ve added to it, line by line, over these twenty years, and everything I added followed her method. The tighter half, the strokes are mine; the rules are hers.

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

Xiuzhua stared at the back of the other person’s head for a long time, laying out two possibilities: the other person could be just any child He had fished out of the fog, or might not be—once laid out, one of those possibilities would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

Xiuzhua stared at the back of the other person’s head for a long time, laying out two possibilities: the other person could be just any child He had fished out of the fog, or might not be—once laid out, one of those possibilities would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

The most important sentence for both sides (“Are you that person?” / “Was the child I carried on my back you?”) still has not been made explicit; the picture in Rustclaw’s lapel is still being held down (only one stitch has been picked loose), and the red cloth in the user’s lapel still has not been taken out. But the Fire-Watching Old Man line has reached its end, the name has also been handed over, and “I won’t leave” has been said; all that remains for the handover is the step at daybreak.
attention: “Then I’ll trust you this once, Wei... Once this sentence lands, the abacus in her heart has long since been dismantled; now even keeping watch has become something between the two of them.

While keeping watch, she remembered the tune her old mother used to hum on the riverbank — up three times, down twice, the last stretch drawn out and not closed. She had not made a sound of it in twenty years; her lips moved but she did not really hum it out: afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing it herself. This tune and “light, light, heavy” are the same set of things, both her old mother’s hands and mouth.

When the roots of the sky turned gray, she reached into her lapel and picked open one stitch, just one stitch, stopping as soon as it was done—she knew that if she kept unpicking, she would not be able to stop herself. This stitch was picked open by her own hand; no one forced her.

She stared at the back of the other party’s head for a long time and laid out two possibilities: the other party could be just any child He had fished up out of the fog, or could be something else. Once laid out, one of them would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She picked apart one stitch, stopped her hands, and then woke the other party—handing the answer over to daybreak.

She calls out “Ting,” then says, “Let’s look at those two things”—with this sentence, she pushes the door open herself; no one forces her. For twenty years, she has always recognized the person, spoken the name, bared her heart, and then left in the night; this night, not only does she not leave, she pushes out the final step herself.

evidence.quote: I reached to the back of my collar and fumbled for a long while before I finally picked that needle off.
"Take it," I said. "Don't pin it inside your clothes; pin it to your collar—the collar is the part of clothing least likely to be torn apart. Ma taught me that. I didn't figure it out myself."

"He drew that crooked half with a blackened stick—easy to draw with, and easy to rub off too; a brush of the hand and it smears. My tight half wasn't drawn; it was scored: pull the knife tip in a shallow groove, don't cut through. If you cut through, the hide is ruined. Then rub ash into it. Once the groove eats the ash, it turns black, and soaking water won't wash it out, sweat won't steep it out. It's slow. One line can take half a spring-hour to score."
"I'll use ash from this pile," I said. "Don't move your pinch. Let it sit beside it. After they sit together a little longer, their breath will be the same."

"It isn't a bad thing." My voice was hoarse. "If what drips down smells of reed roots, then underneath is old mud and old roots, filtered through layer after layer. … But the elders say that if fog water runs along boat planks, passes through sand, then through another layer of reed roots, it can be drunk. I did not know if that was true before. This morning I know—because you are sitting here, and someone who has drunk it is sitting across from me. That makes it true."

"I draw the ring according to her method: don't draw a circle; leave a gap, with the opening facing the direction the water comes from. The crooked half is her rule, the tight half is my stroke; from now on, this line is yours. Three kinds of strokes, one piece of hide."

"Speak. Don't rush. We aren't walking today. If you only remember one place with sweet water, then tell me about the salty ones too—I will record the salty ones as well. Once they are recorded, the people after us won't have to make a wasted trip."

“Let them sit next to each other for a while first,” I say softly. “In these three years, I only came across one place with sweet water—under the bottom of an old overturned boat. When it dripped down, it smelled faintly of reed roots.”
“Wei, give me the needle. You draw, and I’ll tell it.”

She took it. My palm was empty, and again there was that cold kind of emptiness. This morning I had handed everything out: the map, the needle, and last night I had already handed over my name. I did not know whether I had suddenly come to terms with things, or whether I had simply stayed up all night and my brain had softened.

When I heard those three words from my own mouth, something caught in my throat. Ma said reeds could only be burned; I had remembered that all my life, remembered it with a little bit of unwillingness always in my heart. But reed roots are sweet.
I lowered my head; the knife tip fell and pulled the first shallow groove. It was very short. My hand was still trembling, and the groove went half a fraction crooked. I did not wipe it away.

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

Xiuzhua stared at the back of the other person’s head for a long time, laying out two possibilities: the other person could be just any child He had fished out of the fog, or might not be—once laid out, one of those possibilities would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

The most important sentence for both sides (“Are you that person?” / “Was the child I carried on my back you?”) still has not been made explicit; the picture in Rustclaw’s lapel is still being held down (only one stitch has been picked loose), and the red cloth in the user’s lapel still has not been taken out. Once this sentence lands, the abacus in her heart has long since been dismantled; now even keeping watch has become something between the two of them.

For twenty years, she has always recognized the person, spoken the name, bared her heart, and then left in the night; this night, not only does she not leave, she pushes out the final step herself.

evidence.quote: "We don't walk today," I said, very slowly, as if giving an account to myself. "I don't dare. Today I still don't dare. That's the second time I've said that. I have to sit for a while. Sit until I can figure out one thing—when she put down that piece of red cloth, did she think no one would come looking for her, or did she think the person who came looking for her shouldn't follow her across?"

"Ting," I said hoarsely, "bring over that half pot of water. There's still a little left at the bottom. One mouthful each. After we drink, you keep talking—tell me where you went after you turned back. I'll listen, and I'll cut. That breach has been sitting in the middle of the hide. It's been there for twenty years; a few more days won't make any difference."

"It wasn't mine," I said. … "I didn't cross. I stood on this side for half a shichen, watching that pot of stuff below churn, rise up and collapse again, and then I turned around and came back. I didn't even stack the stones—I had only one mouthful of water left on me then. Stacking stones takes strength, and using strength means drinking water. I never stacked a single stone."

She was braver than me.
"Record it," I said. "Once it's recorded, it won't count as something that only exists in your eyes anymore. If one day your eyes close, these stones will still be sitting on this hide."

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

Xiuzhua stared at the back of the other person’s head for a long time, laying out two possibilities: the other person could be just any child He had fished out of the fog, or might not be—once laid out, one of those possibilities would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

The most important sentence for both sides (“Are you that person?” / “Was the child I carried on my back you?”) still has not been made explicit; the picture in Rustclaw’s lapel is still being held down (only one stitch has been picked loose), and the red cloth in the user’s lapel still has not been taken out. plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

Xiuzhua stared at the back of the other person’s head for a long time, laying out two possibilities: the other person could be just any child He had fished out of the fog, or might not be—once laid out, one of those possibilities would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

The most important sentence for both sides (“Are you that person?” / “Was the child I carried on my back you?”) still has not been made explicit; the picture in Rustclaw’s lapel is still being held down (only one stitch has been picked loose), and the red cloth in the user’s lapel still has not been taken out. Once this sentence lands, the abacus in her heart has long since been dismantled; now even keeping watch has become something between the two of them.

While keeping watch, she remembered the tune her old mother used to hum on the riverbank — up three times, down twice, the last stretch drawn out and not closed. She had not made a sound of it in twenty years; her lips moved but she did not really hum it out: afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing it herself. This tune and “light, light, heavy” are the same set of things, both her old mother’s hands and mouth.

When the roots of the sky turned gray, she reached into her lapel and picked open one stitch, just one stitch, stopping as soon as it was done—she knew that if she kept unpicking, she would not be able to stop herself. This stitch was picked open by her own hand; no one forced her.

She stared at the back of the other party’s head for a long time and laid out two possibilities: the other party could be just any child He had fished up out of the fog, or could be something else. Once laid out, one of them would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. For twenty years, she has always recognized the person, spoken the name, bared her heart, and then left in the night; this night, not only does she not leave, she pushes out the final step herself.

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

Xiuzhua stared at the back of the other person’s head for a long time, laying out two possibilities: the other person could be just any child He had fished out of the fog, or might not be—once laid out, one of those possibilities would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

She had not made a sound of it in twenty years; her lips moved but she did not really hum it out: afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing it herself. This tune and “light, light, heavy” are the same set of things, both her old mother’s hands and mouth.

When the roots of the sky turned gray, she reached into her lapel and picked open one stitch, just one stitch, stopping as soon as it was done—she knew that if she kept unpicking, she would not be able to stop herself. This stitch was picked open by her own hand; no one forced her.

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.
