plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

Xiuzhua stared at the back of the other person’s head for a long time, laying out two possibilities: the other person could be just any child He had fished out of the fog, or might not be—once laid out, one of those possibilities would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

The most important sentence for both sides (“Are you that person?” / “Was the child I carried on my back you?”) still has not been made explicit; the picture in Rustclaw’s lapel is still being held down (only one stitch has been picked loose), and the red cloth in the user’s lapel still has not been taken out. But the Fire-Watching Old Man line has reached its end, the name has also been handed over, and “I won’t leave” has been said; all that remains for the handover is the step at daybreak.
attention: “Then I’ll trust you this once, Wei... When it’s light, wake me, and we’ll look at those two things together”—the other party says the word “trust” aloud for the first time, and also asks her not to leave during the night and to call his name once more when he wakes. Once this sentence lands, the abacus in her heart has long since been dismantled; now even keeping watch has become something between the two of them.

While keeping watch, she remembered the tune her old mother used to hum on the riverbank — up three times, down twice, the last stretch drawn out and not closed. She had not made a sound of it in twenty years; her lips moved but she did not really hum it out: afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing it herself. This tune and “light, light, heavy” are the same set of things, both her old mother’s hands and mouth.

When the roots of the sky turned gray, she reached into her lapel and picked open one stitch, just one stitch, stopping as soon as it was done—she knew that if she kept unpicking, she would not be able to stop herself. This stitch was picked open by her own hand; no one forced her.

She stared at the back of the other party’s head for a long time and laid out two possibilities: the other party could be just any child He had fished up out of the fog, or could be something else. Once laid out, one of them would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She picked apart one stitch, stopped her hands, and then woke the other party—handing the answer over to daybreak.

She calls out “Ting,” then says, “Let’s look at those two things”—with this sentence, she pushes the door open herself; no one forces her. For twenty years, she has always recognized the person, spoken the name, bared her heart, and then left in the night; this night, not only does she not leave, she pushes out the final step herself.

The latent vigilance shared by both sides: Rust Claw acknowledged the gesture, said “I believe you now”, answered about Luwan and about keeping watch through three winters, admitted that the thing inside his lapel is half of He’s, and said “I am not leaving”, yet he still keeps the two most important things pressed down—the picture inside his lapel has not been taken out (only one stitch has been picked apart), and “are you that child” has not been asked; the red cloth inside the user's lapel still has not been taken out, and the most important question, “were you the one who carried me”, is still pressed under the tip of the tongue. The escape route has narrowed to only one layer of cloth.

The fire is still burning, and the firewood has been calculated without a moment’s error.

evidence.quote: "I don't dare say this was her." My voice was hoarse. "A mark the wind had rubbed faint; you walked past it a year later, and I am hearing you tell it twenty years later. I know better than anyone how to make things up."
"Go on. After crossing the riverbed and heading northeast—where did you sleep the first night? At what line did the fog stop?"
"The day is still long. There is still a little less than half a can left; save it until after noon before eating. I counted the firewood. There is enough to burn until tomorrow morning."

"The person arranging the stones squatted down. When she got up, her left foot couldn't bear the force, so she had to kick outward with it to rise. What that kick made was a drag mark, from the stones toward the direction she was going."

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

Xiuzhua stared at the back of the other person’s head for a long time, laying out two possibilities: the other person could be just any child He had fished out of the fog, or might not be—once laid out, one of those possibilities would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

Xiuzhua stared at the back of the other person’s head for a long time, laying out two possibilities: the other person could be just any child He had fished out of the fog, or might not be—once laid out, one of those possibilities would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

The most important sentence for both sides (“Are you that person?” / “Was the child I carried on my back you?”) still has not been made explicit; the picture in Rustclaw’s lapel is still being held down (only one stitch has been picked loose), and the red cloth in the user’s lapel still has not been taken out. But the Fire-Watching Old Man line has reached its end, the name has also been handed over, and “I won’t leave” has been said; all that remains for the handover is the step at daybreak.
attention: “Then I’ll trust you this once, Wei... When it’s light, wake me, and we’ll look at those two things together”—the other party says the word “trust” aloud for the first time, and also asks her not to leave during the night and to call his name once more when he wakes. Once this sentence lands, the abacus in her heart has long since been dismantled; now even keeping watch has become something between the two of them.

While keeping watch, she remembered the tune her old mother used to hum on the riverbank — up three times, down twice, the last stretch drawn out and not closed. She had not made a sound of it in twenty years; her lips moved but she did not really hum it out: afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing it herself. This tune and “light, light, heavy” are the same set of things, both her old mother’s hands and mouth.

When the roots of the sky turned gray, she reached into her lapel and picked open one stitch, just one stitch, stopping as soon as it was done—she knew that if she kept unpicking, she would not be able to stop herself. This stitch was picked open by her own hand; no one forced her.

She stared at the back of the other party’s head for a long time and laid out two possibilities: the other party could be just any child He had fished up out of the fog, or could be something else. Once laid out, one of them would turn these twenty years of hers into an entirely different matter. She picked apart one stitch, stopped her hands, and then woke the other party—handing the answer over to daybreak.

She calls out “Ting,” then says, “Let’s look at those two things”—with this sentence, she pushes the door open herself; no one forces her. For twenty years, she has always recognized the person, spoken the name, bared her heart, and then left in the night; this night, not only does she not leave, she pushes out the final step herself.

The escape route has narrowed to only one layer of cloth.

The fire is still burning, and the firewood has been calculated without a moment’s error.

plot_point: A continuation of fireside night talk: two unfamiliar survivors continue exchanging resources and fragments of their pasts beside a fire in the ruins of a gas station. The white fog has already spread to the base of the station's pumps, hugging the ground, while the firelight holds it three steps away.

Xiuzhua kept watch all night—counting firewood (seventeen wooden strips, two handfuls of bark, half a burned door panel), adding fuel to the fire, watching the fog recede (in the latter half of the night, the white fog withdrew from the foot of the oil pump toward lower ground, first revealing the guardrail and then the ruts; when it retreated, there was no sound, like someone slowly lifting a wet cloth from the ground).

While keeping night watch, Rustclaw remembered the tune his old mother used to hum on the riverbank (up three times, down two times, with the last stretch drawn out and left unresolved). He had not made a sound in twenty years; his lips moved, but he did not really hum it—afraid of startling the other person, and also afraid of hearing himself.

When the root of the sky turned gray, Rustclaw reached a hand into the lapel, felt through the cloth that had been patched three times to touch those hard lines (the crooked half, the tight half), used a fingernail to pick apart one stitch, just one stitch, and stopped after picking it apart, without continuing to undo it.

She would have to recalculate who she herself is, and recalculate what exactly she was guarding through those three winters.

The base of the sky turned gray; Xiuzhua pried off the last half door panel and stuffed it into the fire, reached a hand out, stopped half an inch from the other party’s shoulder, then withdrew it and clenched it into a fist, called out “Ting,” “it’s dawn,” and said, “Get up—we’ll look at those two things.”

evidence.quote: "Set up high." I said hoarsely, my eyes looking ahead, looking at the old riverbed’s edge line slowly seeping into view. "So high it was like she was afraid the person she was waiting for wouldn’t see it."

"A high pole isn’t set up for people who have walked right up to it to see. Once you’ve walked right up to it, you can put the cloth on the ground and people will see it just the same. Setting it high is for people far away to see—for the kind of far away where you can’t make out what’s on the ground. She set that up for someone still in the north, someone who still didn’t know which way to go."
"My name is Wei. She was called He. Mother named us on the river shoal—there were only those two things on the shoal. She told people why: grain can be eaten; reeds can only be burned.
"Today we walk only as far as the water." I said. "Today, just to the water."

"Then you tell me about the pole inch by inch." I said hoarsely. "How high the pole was, which section of the top the cloth was tied to, whether it was tied with a dead knot or a slipknot—a slipknot means it was still meant to be untied; a dead knot means she did not plan to come back and untie it. If you saw this clearly, then tell me; if you didn’t, then say you didn’t."
Dry. Prickly, not sticky. This kind of wind will not raise fog early in the night.

“All right, water first. As for the pole, once you’re sitting steady and have had enough to drink, I’ll explain it to you inch by inch.” … “It stands very high, Wei. So high it’s as if it’s afraid the person it’s waiting for won’t see it.”
"She answered Mother back for me. It took her twenty years to let me hear it."

I did not stop, but under my feet I slowed by one beat, then caught up again, catching up half a step faster than before. Half a step—I heard it myself. For twenty years I have never hurried when I walked; people who hurry on the road die early. Today I hurried half a step.

A high pole isn’t set up for people who have walked right up to it to see. Once you’ve walked right up to it, you can put the cloth on the ground and people will see it just the same. Setting it high is for people far away to see—for the kind of far away where you can’t make out what’s on the ground. She set that up for someone still in the north, someone who still didn’t know which way to go.

My name is Wei. She was called He. Mother named us on the river shoal—there were only those two things on the shoal. She told people why: grain can be eaten; reeds can only be burned. She said it her whole life.
On that shoal, He chose the tallest reed, stood it up, and tied that piece of red to it.
She answered Mother back for me. It took her twenty years to let me hear it.

Then tell me about the pole inch by inch. How tall is the pole, which section of it is the cloth tied to, is it tied in a dead knot or a slipknot—a slipknot means it is meant to be untied later; a dead knot means there is no plan to come back and untie it.
Today we’ll just go as far as the water. Today, just to the water.

He was four years younger than me. She was sloppy when she sewed things, but she walked steadier than I did; when she stepped across ice, she made no sound.
Back then, we had a saying: red cloth cannot be taken into the fog and thrown away; it has to be left by the fire. The person left behind counts as still alive, counts as still waiting.
questions: That piece of cloth of yours—when the elder sewed it, did they ever say why it was sewn in?
You came all the way up from the south—did you walk and walk on your own, or... did that old man tell you to go north? Did he ever mention the name of a place?

fabricated_items: About twenty paces west of the broken bridge, there's a flat rock. There are words carved into the stone from before the Fog, but the rain has gnawed them down until only half is left

That half of a white chimney—the old people said that before the Fog, there was a lime kiln underneath it. The smoke was as white as snow, and it burned for decades without stopping. In the year of the Cataclysm, half the kiln collapsed, but the chimney didn't fall. It still stands there now

I kept watch there for three winters. The first year, I added firewood every day. By day I went into collapsed houses to dig out anything that would burn, and at night I retreated to the high slope and watched that little bit of fire—when the fog came down over it, the fire went out, and at daybreak I would go light it again. The second year, I learned to build the fire in the cracks between the stones, so it could last a little longer. The third year... the third year, the water ran out. All the wells around Lu Bay turned salty, so salty even the livestock wouldn't drink. I left.
questions: That old man—is he still there? The fire at the boathouse, was it still burning when you left?
I still don't know what you're called. Did the old man ever give you a name?
in these three years, as you came here from the south, where you passed through, and where the water was sweet.
After we gather them, take out that pinch from the boat house too and let me have a look—not asking you to hand it over, just to look.
from the boat-house, which way do you go to reach that upside-down boat, and how many days' walk?
Was the whole boat bottom-up, or was it turned on its side, pressing down one edge?
Was the ground underneath sand or mud—sand drinks water fast, mud can hold it; the marks drawn for those two are different.
does that water drip all day, or only after the fog retreats at night?

fabricated_items: The batch of old bones who came north from the south called it the 'Mute Bell'—said that before the fog, there used to be a bell hanging from the tower top. When the fog rose, it would ring, and when it rang people ran for high ground. In the year of the catastrophe, the top of the tower blew apart, and the bell fell and was buried in the sand; it never sounded again
questions: How did you cross the two stretches of saline-alkali land—did you go around, or force your way straight through? Did you carry enough water, or did you dig along the way?
These three years, were you always heading north, or did you also detour east?

Was the cloth pressed down, or tied on? Pressed down means 'I'm leaving'; tied on means 'I'll come back.' Were the stones stacked flat, or with the points upward—points upward means they left in a hurry, didn't have time to stack them neatly. And those three stones... was the top one bigger than the two below, or smaller?
tell me where you went after you turned back.

along the ditch northward, what did you see on the first day? Was there water in the ditch, what did the water taste like, and what was that cluster of fire you kept watch over at night built on top of?
Think again—is it a single curve, with three short horizontal strokes underneath? Like three drops of water leaking beneath a crescent moon.
You finished the first day; what about the second—when the gully goes north, does it turn? When you were guarding that cluster of fire, where did the fog stop when it came up?
Say that again. The fog spread to the second crack and stopped—did it stop there that night, or did it stay there the whole night, not climbing up even an inch?
The next day the ditch turned northwest—after it turned, where did you sleep? That night, at what height did the fog stop?
And after the stone pavilion—does the ditch still go northwest? How wide is that layer of moss?
Which year? When you reached that riverbed, was it the first year, the second year, or the third year?
Under those three small stones, had they sunk into the sand or not? How deep was the ring of the sunken mark—level with the stones' waists, or just a shallow trace?
When you finish eating, tell me the rest of that riverbed—how wide the riverbed was, which way it went, whether the stones were on this bank or that bank.
Which way was it going—from the fine stones toward the northeast, or from the northeast toward the fine stones?
After crossing the riverbed and heading northeast—where did you sleep the first night? At what line did the fog stop?
along that road, how many more places did you see where stones had been arranged? Not carved—arranged. However many there were, just say however many—even one counts.
That first water source of yours—can we reach it by noon?
Tell me about that reed marsh—is it standing in a ditch, or on a shoal? When it sounds, does the sound push from one end to the other, or does the whole stretch sound at once?

How high the pole was, which section of the top the cloth was tied to, whether it was tied with a dead knot or a slipknot—a slipknot means it was still meant to be untied; a dead knot means she did not plan to come back and untie it. If you saw this clearly, then tell me; if you didn’t, then say you didn’t.
